schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch place the search in the house of the books at Babylon where the treasures lay; Ellicott corrects 'made a decree' to 'gave an order' and 'laid up' to 'laid down' in a document-chamber.

Matthew Henry reads the errand as providence: the tribes kept no authentic copy and had to appeal to the original; Darius did not use its absence to rule against the Jews, for out of the eater came forth meat.
Clarke glosses the 'house of the rolls' as the king's library, the first mention of a library in Scripture; Wesley traces the search from Babylon to Achmetha.
Gill takes the decree as an order to search the public records for the edict of Cyrus.

themes: the search of the imperial archives
the house of the rolls / king's library

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch identify Achmetha as Ecbatana, capital of Great Media built by Dejokes, summer seat of the Persian kings near Hamadan; Ellicott suggests the Babylon original was destroyed by Smerdis and only a Chaldean copy survived at Ecbatana.
Gill refutes the old idea (Jarchi, Aben Ezra) that Achmetha was a chest or vessel: it is a place, Ecbatana, the Median summer residence, its name drawn from heat.
Clarke and Wesley agree Achmetha is Ecbatana, the royal summer city of the Medes and Persians, whither the records of Cyrus had been carried.

Keil and Delitzsch give the decree in full — a place of sacrifice, foundations strongly laid, sixty cubits high and broad; Ellicott hears Isaiah 44:28 behind 'strongly laid' and a term for solid support.
Clarke notes the second temple was much larger than Solomon's; Wesley harmonizes by the sacred cubit, or by referring the sixty cubits to the porch only, and reads 'breadth' as possibly 'length.'

debates.question: How are the sixty-cubit dimensions to be squared with Solomon's temple?

sides.position: the second temple was simply ordered on a larger scale than the first
reconcile the figures by the larger sacred cubit, or by referring the height to the porch alone

themes: a pagan king specifying the sanctuary

schools.summary: Clarke describes three courses of stone bound by a course of timber, and distinguishes what Cyrus paid (timber from Lebanon to Joppa, and the sacrifices) from the general cost, which the Jews bore themselves.
Matthew Henry notes the Jews never received what the decree ordered from the royal revenue, the face of the court being soon changed after Cyrus.
Gill reports Jarchi's reading of the three rows as the walls, and the great stones as marble.
Keil and Delitzsch take the clause as Cyrus's pledge that the cost be met out of the royal house.

themes: three rows of stone and timber

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch read 'to its place' as distributive, each vessel to its own station (cf. Ezra 1:7; Ezra 5:14); Ellicott sees the restoration as an expiation of Belshazzar's desecration (Daniel 5:2-3) and marks the emphatic doubled 'house of God.'
Gill notes the decree confirms what the Jews had told Tatnai, that Cyrus commanded the vessels restored.
Henry reads the warrant to return the vessels, the priests charged to set them all in their places, so those who would control the priests are now at their command.

Ellicott marks the abrupt entry into Darius's decree, framed with Jewish help, and reads 'be ye far from thence' as keeping aloof from interference; Keil and Delitzsch summarize the charge not to hinder but to promote and fund the work.
Henry hears in the wording that Darius knew the officers meant to hinder — 'Be ye far hence' — the wrath of the enemy made to praise God, the remainder restrained.
Gill names Tatnai (whom Josephus calls master of the horse), Shetharboznai and companions beyond the Euphrates.
Clarke: do not interrupt the Jews, but further them to the utmost.
Keil and Delitzsch: the verb means to let the work go on unhindered; the decree names the governor (Sheshbazzar/Zerubbabel) and, with special emphasis, the elders as builders in the temple's place.
Henry finds the decree explicit and satisfactory: Darius forbids opposition and betrays that he knew the officers wished to hinder the work.
Gill reads a plain permission and suspects some had stirred up the officers to molest the builders.

Keil and Delitzsch: the cost is paid from the royal moneys, the tribute beyond the river, punctually and in full so the work not cease; Ellicott stresses the sums are deducted from the very tribute owed to Persia.
Gill takes this as an additional decree granting more than Cyrus, though he records Josephus's view that it merely confirmed Cyrus's edict.
Henry marvels that God's priests should have such an interest in the public money, and that those who would control the work are now at the builders' command.

debates.question: Is Darius's grant a fresh decree or only a confirmation of Cyrus's?

sides.position: an additional decree, granting more than Cyrus had and encouraging the work
no more than a confirmation of what Cyrus had already ordained

themes: the empire pays for the sanctuary

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch read 'day by day without fail' as a guarantee the supply never lapse; Ellicott admires the accuracy of the list (cf. Exodus 29; Leviticus 2) and infers the decree was drawn under good instruction.
Gill notes these were the appointed materials of the burnt offering.
Henry: Darius supplied everything for burnt- and meat-offerings, a standing charge on his revenue, paid daily without fail.

themes: a pagan king maintaining the altar

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch: Darius, like Cyrus (Ezra 1:2), owns Jahve as God of heaven without renouncing polytheism, and seeks his blessing on the dynasty; Ellicott finds two ends — God honoured and the king interceded for (Jeremiah 29:7) — and renders 'sweet savours' as incense (Daniel 2:46).
Clarke notes even a heathen believed prayers to the God of the Jews would avail, a motive that has moved states to tolerate religions for the benefit of their prayers.
Henry lists the honours Darius pays — to God, to his ministers, to prayer — and the duty to pray for those in authority.
Gill: the sacrifices are such as will be acceptable to God.

themes: prayer for the life of the king

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch describe a beam torn from the offender's house, the man fastened and raised on it — impalement, customary among Assyrians and Persians (Herodotus, Nineveh monuments); Ellicott distinguishes Persian crucifixion (nailing after decapitation) from Assyrian impalement and refers 'set up' to the man.
Gill glosses 'alter this word' as acting contrary to the command, changing or revoking it.
Clarke leaves the mode uncertain — hanging, gibbeting, or empaling — inclining to a stake through the body, and reads the dunghill as reduction to unclean ruins.
Henry: hanged before his own door on a beam of his own house, and, as an execrable man, his house made a dunghill.

debates.question: What manner of death penalty does the decree prescribe?

sides.position: impalement or transfixion on a stake, after the Assyrian custom
crucifixion — among the Persians, nailing the body to a cross after decapitation

themes: the death penalty for altering the decree

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch: 'the God who has caused his name to dwell there' is unmistakably biblical (Deuteronomy 12:11), from the Jewish historian's pen, though the imprecation recalls the close of Darius's own Bisitun inscription invoking Ahuramazda.
Gill: Darius speaks of a God who grants his presence and causes his Majesty to dwell there, as in Solomon's temple.
Wesley conjectures the Romans, instruments of the temple's later destruction, felt the effects of Darius's curse, the empire declining ever after.
Henry: what Darius could not do himself he asked of God, to whom vengeance belongs, and shares Wesley's surmise about Rome's decline.

outliers.note: Traces the fall of Rome to Darius's imprecation: the Romans who destroyed the temple felt the curse, and their empire sensibly declined ever after until wholly destroyed — a speculation Henry shares.

themes: God's name dwelling in the temple
the divine avenger of the house

schools.summary: Henry relishes the reversal: the Jews' enemies made their friends, hastening to assist the work as their predecessors had hastened to stop it (Ezra 4:23); the king's moderation made them moderate too.
Keil and Delitzsch stress the diligence with which Tatnai executed Darius's command, speedily and to the letter.
Gill: having received and read the king's letter, they did as bidden.

Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott explain that 'Artaxerxes' can only be Longimanus, named though he reigned after the temple's completion because of his later edict (Ezra 7); Ellicott notes he alone is styled 'king of Persia,' showing Ezra writes in his reign.

Wesley: the success is ascribed not to chance or Darius's good humour but to God, who by his prophets urged the work and disposed the king's heart; Clarke lays out the chronology of Cyrus, Darius, and Artaxerxes.
Gill: the elders went on with the building.
Henry: the elders built cheerfully — bound by God's commandment, shamed by heathen kings, encouraged by Haggai and Zechariah; 'as for God, his work is perfect.'

themes: the prophesying of Haggai and Zechariah

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch parse 'was finished' and note the apocryphal Esdras reads the twenty-third rather than the third day; Ellicott dates completion to Adar, winter 516-515 BC, four years and some months from the resumption (Haggai 1:15), twenty-one years from the first foundation (Ezra 3:10).
Gill identifies Adar as the twelfth month, part of February and March.
Clarke sets the sixth year of Darius about the year of the world 3489, twenty years after Zerubbabel laid the foundation.

themes: the date of completion (Adar, sixth year of Darius)
the long span since the foundation
the third vs twenty-third day variant

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch set out the offerings and the twelve he-goats for all Israel, the temple being for the whole covenant people whose return the prophets foretold (Ezekiel 37:15; Jeremiah 31:27); Ellicott marks the fit title 'children of the captivity' beside the coming 'all Israel.'
Henry dwells on the mingled dignity and poverty of the assembly — some of every tribe, yet now 'the children of the captivity,' a remnant only (Isaiah 7:3).
Gill takes 'the children of Israel' to include the ten tribes remaining or returned, so the dedication was not of Judah alone.

themes: the twelve he-goats for all Israel
the temple for the whole covenant people

schools.summary: Ellicott stresses the people are now 'all Israel,' and that though a single kid was the usual sin offering for the people, only here is one offered for each tribe.

Henry: small beside Solomon's thousands, yet accepted, their deep poverty abounding to liberality (2 Corinthians 8:2); atonement made tribe by tribe lest iniquity be a worm at the root of their comforts.
Gill calls these hecatombs, grand sacrifices even among the heathen (Homer), burnt and peace offerings feasted with gladness.
Clarke: the twelve he-goats were a sin offering for every tribe, one for each.

themes: a sin offering per tribe for all Israel

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch: priests and Levites set by classes to serve each in its week (2 Chronicles 23:4; 2 Kings 11:9), and here the Aramaic section closes (so also Clarke); Ellicott notes the courses were of David's time and the restoration imperfect, the orders not in full number.
Gill: all placed in their proper classes and courses to do the temple's work in turn.
Henry: having dedicated the house they settled the household, making the book of Moses their rule; poorer than Solomon's day but as pure — no beauty like the beauty of holiness.

themes: priests and Levites set in courses
the book of Moses as rule
the close of the Aramaic section

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch read the passover as testimony that regular worship was now carried on in the new temple, weeks after the dedication; Ellicott notes Ezra returns to Hebrew, the feast a renewal of the redemption from Egypt after another wilderness passed.
Gill: the month Nisan/Abib, just after the temple's completion, the passover kept at the exact time the law commanded.
Henry: newly freed from Babylon, it was seasonable to commemorate the deliverance from Egypt; kept 'after a sort' each year, but now with due solemnity in the finished house.

themes: the passover at the appointed time
the two exoduses answering one another

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch: the priests and Levites purified without exception, fit to kill the passover for laity, priests, and themselves; Ellicott translates 'purified as one man,' surpassing Hezekiah's celebration (2 Chronicles 29:34; 2 Chronicles 30:3), the Levites now slaying all the lambs.
Gill: all purified together as one man, more generally prepared than in Hezekiah's day.
Clarke: all ready and clean at one time, needing no second passover for the defiled or distant.
Henry: where Hezekiah's priests lay under blame, these were purified together, unanimous; the purity and unity of ministers adds to the beauty of their service.

Ellicott denies these are heathen proselytes, reading them as the Jewish remnant of the land who had consorted with the foreign populations and now separated (intermarriages recur through Ezra and Nehemiah); Keil and Delitzsch describe the separation from the heathen races to seek Jahve.
Clarke reads them as proselytes won by the captives' good example, drawn to walk in the light of the Lord; Wesley takes 'children of Israel' as probably some of each of the twelve tribes.
Gill: the eaters were Judah and Benjamin with some of the ten tribes mingled among them.
Henry, siding with converts, describes true separation from sin and fellowship with sinners, joining the Israel of God — strangers welcome to the gospel feast.

debates.question: Who are the 'such as had separated themselves' that ate the passover?

sides.position: Gentile proselytes / converts won by the exiles' example
the Jewish remnant of the land, separating from heathen entanglements they had contracted

themes: the open door of the passover
seeking the LORD God of Israel

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch: the Lord made them joyful by turning the king's heart and strengthening their hands, the 'king of Assyria' being Darius as ruler of the former Assyrian realm; Ellicott reads the title as a remembrancer of the oppression under his forerunners.

Clarke, with Calmet, takes 'king of Assyria' for the king of Persia, heir of the Assyrian kings, and notes Darius married two daughters of Cyrus; Wesley reads the title as emphatic, magnifying God's power in turning the hearts of monarchs whose predecessors persecuted his people.
Gill: the feast of unleavened bread immediately followed the passover, as the law prescribed.

Henry: God gave cause and hearts to rejoice; the old men who wept at the first temple were now mostly dead, so no tears mingled with the joy — a token for good when foes prove friends (Proverbs 16:7).

themes: 'king of Assyria' for the king of Persia
God turning the hearts of kings
